mcqs.question: According to the answer skeleton, when should a relationship be embedded rather than referenced?
options: Whenever the related entity has fewer than five total fields
Whenever the database in use technically supports embedding, regardless of the relationship shape
Whenever the parent document is queried more often than the related entity
When it's one-to-few, rarely changes, and is consistently read together with its parent
mcqs.explanation: Embedding fits relationships that are one-to-few, stable, and read alongside their parent — the order line-items case. Field count, technical support for embedding, or relative query frequency of the parent don't determine the right choice on their own.

mcqs.question: How does a NoSQL data model typically represent a many-to-many relationship, like tags on posts?
options: Using a separate join collection storing pairs of related IDs, queried with two lookups instead of a single join
By embedding every tag's full document inside every post document that uses it
Many-to-many relationships cannot be represented in any NoSQL data model
By storing a single shared array field that every post and every tag both reference directly
mcqs.explanation: A join collection mirrors a relational join table, storing pairs of IDs and requiring two lookups to resolve either direction of the relationship. Embedding every tag into every post would duplicate data extensively; many-to-many is representable in NoSQL, just via this pattern rather than a native join; there's no such single shared array approach used in practice.

mcqs.question: What is the trade-off between embedding and referencing that should be named explicitly?
options: Embedding is always slower to read than referencing, in every case
Embedding is fast to read but duplicates data and complicates updates; referencing avoids duplication but pushes join logic into application code
Referencing eliminates the need for any application-level error handling
Embedding can only be used with relational databases, never with document stores
mcqs.explanation: Embedding trades update complexity and duplication for fast reads; referencing avoids duplication but requires the application to perform the join itself. Embedding is actually fast to read, not slow; referencing doesn't remove the need for error handling; and embedding is a document-store technique, not a relational one.

mcqs.question: Why is embedding an unbounded, frequently-changing relationship considered a pitfall?
options: It's actually the recommended default for all relationships regardless of size or change frequency
Growth or change moves or duplicates unnecessary data on every operation, and can eventually hit a hard document size limit
Document databases reject any write that includes more than one embedded relationship
It permanently disables the ability to reference any other entity from that document
mcqs.explanation: An embedded relationship that keeps growing or changing independently means every read and write moves more data than necessary, and document size limits can eventually be hit outright. This is exactly the pattern to avoid, not the recommended default; document databases don't impose such a one-relationship rule, and embedding one relationship doesn't block referencing another.
